analysis.one_liner: Lets any American buy into Medicare instead of private health insurance.
analysis.headline: A bill letting anyone buy into Medicare was referred to committee and died there with no vote and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Alan Grayson's bill would have let any U.S. citizen or legal permanent resident enroll in Medicare by paying a premium, with premiums calculated by age group rather than at senior rates. The Medicare coverage would have counted as qualifying insurance under the Affordable Care Act and qualified for the law's premium subsidies. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, received no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone without Medicare — chiefly working-age adults and children — could have bought government-run Medicare coverage instead of a private plan, with premiums calculated from the actual cost of care for their own age group rather than blended with seniors'. People already on private plans would have gained an outside option, and marketplace shoppers could have applied their ACA premium subsidies to the public plan. No entitlement to benefits would have started before the first calendar year after enactment.

how_it_helps.text: It creates a universal Medicare buy-in: every U.S. citizen or permanent resident not already entitled to Medicare could enroll, with premiums set by age cohort rather than pooled with seniors' rates.
Buying into Medicare would count as minimum essential coverage under the ACA individual mandate, so enrolling would satisfy the requirement to have insurance.
The buy-in would count as a qualified health plan for ACA premium tax credits, so people eligible for premium assistance could use those credits toward the public plan.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would have lost customers to a cheaper public option, and hospitals and doctors treating the new enrollees would have been paid Medicare rates, which are typically lower than private insurance rates. Taxpayers bore no direct new cost since the plan was to be financed by premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not guarantee that the buy-in premium would be affordable: it sets premiums on an actuarial basis by age cohort, with no cap tied to income (unlike the ACA marketplace's income-based subsidies), so a family's premium could still be large.

The public plan would compete directly with private insurers in every market, and critics warned a government-run plan priced from Medicare costs could undercut private plans and push insurers out, leaving the government plan dominant.

Hospitals and doctors worry that expanding Medicare enrollment shifts patients into Medicare payment rates, which are lower than many private insurance rates, potentially reducing revenues at providers already operating on thin margins.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given uninsured and separately insured people a straightforward, administred public insurance option priced by age, likely cheaper than many private plans. The real drawbacks are that premiums set on an age-cohort actuarial basis would not be subsidized for higher earners (unlike marketplace plans), that a large public plan could draw healthier enrollees and strain private insurers' risk pools (which insurers and many economists argue would destabilize markets), and that shifting people to Medicare could affect provider reimbursement rates that hospitals say are already below cost. On balance it was a meaningful consumer option with real design questions, and it never received an assessment through any hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never held a markup or sent it to the floor, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 3737 was introduced on December 12, 2013 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The action history shows no further activity: no hearings, no markup, no vote.
Not a single member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill expired with the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, who kept the individual market to themselves with no public Medicare option competing for customers, are better off because the bill died. So are incumbent members of both parties, who faced no vote on the issue.

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, the only supporter on record.

against.name: Private health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed public-option proposals of this era as unfair government competition with private insurers, and no member of either party advanced this bill beyond referral.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member cosponsored, so no party breakdown exists; the sponsor was a Democrat in a Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: The bill would create a public Medicare option competing directly with private plans in every market, letting people leave private coverage for Medicare. The bill died in committee, so insurers' market position was untouched.

More patients routed into Medicare means more reimbursement at Medicare rates, which are generally lower than private insurance rates. Providers neither campaigned on this bill nor acted on it in the record.
